Simulate Time-to-Event Data via In-Solver Event Detection

Source: R/sim_tte_ode.R
sim_tte_ode.Rd

The event/censoring time is located during ODE integration (at the solver's own internal evaluations), by drawing a per-subject \(U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and integrating the survival probability p11 as a state, latching the first solver time at which p11 <= U. This is a different mechanism from sim_tte/sim_tte_df, which resolve event times after the fact from an already-materialized trajectory – the two are separate code paths, not two modes of one function.

Usage

sim_tte_ode(
  model,
  param = list(),
  omega = NULL,
  sigma = NULL,
  n = 1L,
  end = 100,
  delta = 1,
  add = NULL,
  idata = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  beta = NULL,
  formula = NULL,
  knots = NULL,
  boundary_knots = NULL,
  coefs = NULL,
  censoring = NULL,
  visits = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  keep_trajectory = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

model

What to simulate. One of: a character name from sim_tte_ode_models() ("exponential", "weibull", "gompertz", "mspline", "pk_hazard", "irm1_hazard"–"irm4_hazard", "tmdd_hazard"); a "simtte_model" returned by tte_model (your own converted mrgsolve model); or the "simtte_prepared_model" returned by simtte_prepare_model, for parallel or multi-process use. A bare compiled mrgmod is not accepted: convert it with tte_model first.

param

Named list or named numeric vector of population-level $PARAM overrides, forwarded to param. U and END are ordinarily supplied per subject via idata (see below), not here.

omega

Optional square matrix. For a model that already declares a matching $OMEGA block (any user-supplied model with its own ETA() wiring), forwarded to omat as before. For a built-in PK/PD hazard-library model with no declared block, applied instead as per-subject between-subject variability via idata columns – see "Between-subject variability" below.

sigma

Optional square matrix, forwarded to smat. User-model-only: no built-in library model's hazard depends on a residual-error-perturbed quantity, so there is no idata-based analogue for sigma.

n

Integer. Number of subjects. Ignored (and inferred from nrow(idata)) when idata is supplied. Also ignored (and inferred from nrow(covariates) instead) when idata is NULL and a baseline, no-ID formula covariate frame (see "Covariates and the linear predictor" below) has more than one row – supplying n explicitly in that case is only valid if it matches that row count exactly (an error names both numbers otherwise). When a dosing data with an ID column is also supplied, n (or idata's row count) must equal length(unique(data$ID)) exactly – inferred from it when n/idata are both left unresolved, checked otherwise (an error names both numbers; see data below).

end

Numeric scalar. Administrative censoring horizon. Written into the model's END parameter for every subject that does not already supply its own END column in idata, and used to guard in-solver event detection against latching a time past the requested follow-up (see "Boundary guard" below).

delta

Numeric scalar. Reported-grid spacing, used to build the requested output grid seq(0, end, by = delta) when add is not supplied. Ignored if add is supplied.

add

Numeric vector of explicit reported times. If NULL (default), seq(0, end, by = delta) is used. Either way, end itself is always included in the resolved grid (via .resolve_output_grid()), which the censoring rule and refinement step below both depend on.

idata

NULL (default) or a data frame with an ID column and, optionally, U and/or END columns. Missing U is drawn as stats::runif(nrow(idata)) (one independent draw per row/subject; see "Reproducibility" below). Missing END is filled with end. Any other column is passed through to mrgsolve as an ordinary per-subject covariate/parameter.

data

Optional dosing event data, forwarded to mrgsim's own data argument. If covariates is also supplied, the covariate-update rows built from it are appended to data (see "Covariates and the linear predictor" below); either or both may be NULL. When supplied together with more than one resolved subject, data must have an ID column whose unique values equal the resolved subject set (from n/idata) exactly – every subject dosed via data must have exactly one idata/ n row, and vice versa (an error, checked before simulating, names any mismatch and the fix). Before this check existed, n exceeding data's own ID count silently dropped the extra subjects from the result with no warning, and n short of it failed with mrgsolve's own opaque "ID found in the data set, but not in idata" – both now error immediately from here instead.

covariates

NULL (default) or a covariate data frame, either baseline (one row per subject, no time column) or time-varying (a time column, an optional ID column, and one numeric column per covariate) – see "Covariates and the linear predictor" below. Required together with beta; an error if only one of the two is supplied.

beta

NULL (default) or a named numeric vector of log-linear coefficients. Without formula, one name per raw column of covariates (lp(t) = sum(beta * covariates(t)), the original interface, unchanged). With formula, one name per column of the design matrix formula implies (lp(t) = X(t) %*% beta) – see "Covariates and the linear predictor" below.

formula

NULL (default, preserving the original covariates/beta behaviour exactly) or a one-sided formula, e.g. ~ age + arm, built into a design matrix via model.matrix against covariates. See "Covariates and the linear predictor" below.

knots, boundary_knots, coefs

Only used (and, together with coefs, required) when model = "mspline"; an error if any is supplied for another model. knots: numeric vector of interior knots, strictly increasing, strictly inside boundary_knots – its length selects which shipped knot-count variant is used (see "M-spline knot-count variants" below). boundary_knots: numeric c(lower, upper), default c(0, end). coefs: numeric vector of non-negative M-spline coefficients, length length(knots) + 3 (2 = spline degree, fixed).

censoring

NULL (default) or a censoring spec list (see add_censoring). When supplied, an independent censoring time is drawn per subject and applied to $events via add_censoring, inside this call's own seeded block – see "Right censoring" below.

visits

NULL (default), a visit schedule (a numeric vector or per-subject data frame, see add_interval_censoring), or a jitter spec list(every = <spacing>, jitter = <optional>, jitter_dist = <optional, "uniform"/"normal">, jitter_trunc = <optional>). When supplied, add_interval_censoring is applied to $events after any censoring above – see "Interval censoring" below. The jitter-spec form calls visit_schedule internally, inside this call's own seeded block (add_interval_censoring itself does not accept this third form).

seed

Optional integer. If supplied, set.seed(seed) is called before U is drawn.

keep_trajectory

Logical. If TRUE, the full mrgsim() output is retained in the returned object's $trajectory. Default FALSE (the coarse-output/in-solver-detection design is partly motivated by not requiring a dense materialized trajectory for large cohorts).

...

Forwarded to mrgsim. tgrid, obsonly, nocb, and carry_out/carry.out are controlled internally to guarantee the contracts documented here and cannot be overridden; supplying them raises an error naming the argument (the same .check_reserved_dots() mechanism sim_tte already uses). This is where solver-tolerance arguments relevant to in-solver event-time accuracy (rtol, atol, hmax, ...) are set.

Value

An object of class "simtte_ode_sim", a list with:

events

Data frame with columns ID, sim_time, sim_status (1 = event, 0 = censored), sim_reason ("event", "censored", or "administrative" – see "Right censoring" below); plus sim_time_left/ sim_time_right when visits is supplied (see "Interval censoring" below).

trajectory

The full mrgsim() output data frame, or NULL unless keep_trajectory = TRUE.

model

The compiled mrgmod object used.

seed

The seed argument, as supplied (possibly NULL).

call

The matched call, for reproducibility bookkeeping.

Details

Typical order of use: pick a model (a built-in name from sim_tte_ode_models, or convert your own mrgsolve model with tte_model first), call this function, then optionally post-process the $events it returns with add_censoring and add_interval_censoring (or pass censoring/visits to do both in this call).

The sections below follow one reading order: the mechanism itself ("Boundary guard", "Event-time refinement"), then what varies by model ("Weibull shape support", "M-spline knot-count variants", "PK/PD-linked hazard models"), then the cross-cutting inputs any model can take ("Covariates and the linear predictor", "Between-subject variability", "Right censoring", "Interval censoring"), and finally "Reproducibility", which ties every draw above together.

model %in% c("exponential", "weibull", "gompertz") are the three closed-hazard-form library models; model = "mspline" is the flexible baseline hazard (see "M-spline knot-count variants" below); "pk_hazard", "irm1_hazard"–"irm4_hazard", and "tmdd_hazard" are the six PK/PD-linked models (see "PK/PD-linked hazard models" below). model may also be a simtte_model produced by tte_model, which converts a user's own mrgsolve PK/PD model into one usable here – see tte_model's own documentation, or sim_tte_ode_models to list the built-in names programmatically. A bare compiled mrgmod is not accepted directly; convert it first.

Boundary guard

the administrative-censoring contract: The shipped library models latch TEVT (the in-solver event time) only while SOLVERTIME <= END, so an internal solver evaluation past the requested follow-up horizon can never be recorded as an event time. sim_tte_ode() additionally re-applies the boundary rule on the R side, independent of the in-model guard: a subject is censored (sim_status = 0, sim_time = end) if no event was latched at all, or if the latched time is >= end. This is deliberately belt-and-braces: the in-model guard is an internal robustness measure; the R-side rule above is the documented contract.

Event-time refinement

The raw in-solver TEVT is quantized to the ODE solver's own internal step grid, which is generally finer than, but not independent of, the requested output grid and solver tolerance. For every subject classified as an event, sim_tte_ode() therefore refines the final sim_time using the already-validated cumulative-hazard interpolation .interpolate_log_survival() (the same method sim_tte_df offers as event_time_method = "log_survival"), applied between the solver's own last pre-crossing evaluation and the crossing evaluation itself – an interval one internal solver step wide, captured directly from the model, not between the two reported trajectory rows bracketing U. TEVT itself therefore only decides whether a subject had an event before end; the reported sim_time for an event subject comes from this bracket interpolation, not from the raw TEVT value.

This makes refinement accuracy independent of delta/ add: because the bracket is a solver step, not a reporting interval, its width (and hence the constant-hazard-within-bracket approximation error) does not grow as the requested output grid gets coarser – confirmed directly across delta of 4, 1, and 0.25 for Weibull shape = 0.5, 1, 2, 5 and Gompertz gamma = +/-, where an earlier, grid-based refinement approach had instead gotten worse than raw TEVT at coarse delta for shapes far from 1. delta/add therefore now control only the resolution of the returned $trajectory (when keep_trajectory = TRUE) and of the reported-grid fallback described next – not the accuracy of a refined event time.

The reported-grid method is kept only as a fallback, used for a subject when the in-solver bracket is degenerate (its pre-crossing evaluation coincides with, or is not earlier than, the crossing itself; p11(0) = 1 > U for every valid U < 1 rules this out at t = 0 specifically, but it is not ruled out later in integration – see the next paragraph) or unavailable (a user-supplied trajectory missing the T_PRE/P_PRE/ P_POST capture columns). One message() is emitted per sim_tte_ode() call whenever any subject falls back, naming how many did; a finer delta/add improves those subjects' event times specifically (the fallback is exactly the earlier grid-based method, so its accuracy still depends on the grid). This message never changes the returned result and is suppressible with suppressMessages(), like every guardrail message this function emits (see also "Weibull shape support" below).

Two fallback-triggering mechanisms have been characterized so far, with different remedies, and the message differentiates them (classified purely from the already-captured bracket columns, no new model-side logic): a Weibull-type signature (P_POST outside [0, 1], a genuine solver overshoot across one large internal step, remedied by a finer delta/add), and an M-spline-type signature (T_PRE == TEVT exactly, with both P_PRE and P_POST legitimate probabilities – a same-timestamp, multiple-corrector-iteration degeneracy near a locally steep hazard, remedied by tighter rtol/atol, not delta). A subject matching neither signature (including every subject when the bracket columns are unavailable at all) is reported as unclassified, with generic advice. Only the non-zero buckets are named in the message.

A very steep hazard at a coarse delta can trigger this fallback for an entire cohort at once: mrgsolve/lsoda does not take an internal solver step past the next requested output time, so a coarse delta can force one large internal step across a region where the hazard changes by orders of magnitude, and a trial/corrector evaluation partway through that step can be momentarily unphysical – detected and safely handled by the fallback described above, not a silent wrong answer. Measured directly for Weibull shape = 5 and shape = 10: fallback engagement drops from 100% of subjects to 0% between delta = 1 and delta = 0.5 at shape = 10. The remedy is exactly what the fallback message already states: request a finer delta/add. This is a named, disclosed, non-blocking regime, not a separate guardrail.

Weibull shape support

The closed-form sim_tte's Weibull model has no restriction on shape (an exact analytical expression is evaluated at every reported time). This function's "weibull" library model genuinely integrates the Weibull hazard as an ODE state, which diverges as \(t \to 0^+\) for shape < 1 – a real mathematical property of the hazard, not a floating-point artifact (integrating this exact hazard as an ODE fails outright for small shapes without a floor). weibull_ode.cpp floors the time value used inside the hazard expression only (never SOLVERTIME itself) at 1e-100, which was verified directly to eliminate solver failure/NaN/non-monotone p11 entirely across shape from 0.01 to 10, with accuracy at or below mrgsolve's own default solver tolerance for shape >= 0.05, degrading gracefully (larger but still finite, still monotone bias) below that. This model always runs (no error) for any shape > 0; for shape < 0.05 specifically, prefer sim_tte(type = "weibull") if exactness near t = 0 matters more than the in-solver mechanism's other properties. sim_tte_ode() additionally emits one message() per call when the effective shape (after param overrides) is below 0.05, pointing back to this section; the simulation itself is unaffected (suppressible with suppressMessages(), like the refinement-fallback message described above).

M-spline knot-count variants

model = "mspline" evaluates a degree-2 (quadratic) normalized M-spline basis (Ramsay 1988 scaling, matching splines2::mSpline(..., degree = 2, intercept = TRUE) exactly – verified to floating-point precision) inside the compiled model, in C++, not as a precomputed covariate the way sim_tte(type = "ms") does: HAZ = eta * sum_m coefs[m] * M_m(t), a genuinely continuous, smooth hazard, integrated as a real $ODE state like every other sim_tte_ode() model (chosen specifically so the in-solver bracket refinement above, which assumes a smooth hazard, applies to the M-spline model too – a piecewise-constant covariate does not give that).

Because the basis is compiled in, only a small, fixed set of interior-knot counts is shipped (3, 5, or 7 interior knots, a moderate, fixed-set compromise) – length(knots) selects which shipped variant is used; any other count errors, naming the supported counts and pointing to sim_tte(type = "ms"), which accepts an arbitrary knot count (at the cost of being a piecewise-constant hazard on its own reporting grid, not a continuous one). knots (interior), boundary_knots (c(lower, upper), default c(0, end)), and coefs (length length(knots) + 3, non-negative – the basis itself is non-negative, so a negative coefficient would make the hazard negative) together define the same hazard sim_tte(type = "ms") would produce from a splines2::mSpline() basis built with the same knots/degree and coefs as its own coefs argument – knots and coefficients are directly portable between the two functions.

No time floor is needed (unlike "weibull"'s divergence at t = 0): the M-spline basis is bounded and finite everywhere on [boundary_knots[1], boundary_knots[2]], including exactly at the boundary – verified directly, not assumed. The hazard is identically zero outside that interval, though (a consequence of the clamped-knot spline construction): end (and every idata$END) must not exceed boundary_knots[2], enforced as an error, not a silent extrapolation – the same restriction sim_tte(type = "ms")'s own end_time > max(time) check already applies, for the same reason.

Simulating from a Cox model

A Cox model specifies \(h(t \mid X) = h_0(t) \exp(X\beta)\) but leaves the baseline \(h_0(t)\) unspecified, so simulating from one requires choosing a baseline. model = "mspline" supplies a flexible one: its hazard is exp(mu + lp) * sum_m coefs[m] * M_m(t), i.e. \(h_0(t) = e^{\mu} \sum_m c_m M_m(t)\) with covariates entering multiplicatively through lp = X %*% beta (see "Covariates and the linear predictor" below). The simulated data therefore satisfy proportional hazards exactly, and survival::coxph() fitted to them estimates beta. See vignette("pkpd-time-to-event", package = "simtte") for a worked example recovering beta this way.

PK/PD-linked hazard models

Six library models link the hazard to a PK/PD quantity computed by a genuine mrgsolve PK/PD backbone, each reusing an unedited mrgsolve::modlib() model verbatim and adding only the survival scaffold and the hazard link itself (the per-model mechanical-edit list is documented at the top of each .cpp file, and is exactly what tte_model automates for a model of your own):

  • "pk_hazard" (backbone "pk2cmt"): concentration- driven, log-linear: HAZ = H0 * exp(beta_cp * CP).

  • "irm1_hazard"–"irm4_hazard" (backbones "irm1"–"irm4", the four indirect-response types): response-driven, relative to the subject's own pre-dose baseline: HAZ = H0 * exp(beta_r * (RESP / RESP0 - 1)), where RESP0 = KIN / KOUT. The sign of beta_r gives the direction (positive: a response above baseline raises the hazard; negative: it lowers it).

  • "tmdd_hazard" (backbone "tmdd"): linked to RC, the drug-target complex, not to free drug concentration – chosen because RC is the quantity unique to target-mediated disposition (a CP-based link would not differ in kind from "pk_hazard"); HAZ = H0 * exp(beta_rc * RC).

Every one of the six reduces exactly to the exponential model with hazard H0 when its beta_* parameter is 0. Dosing and other event data are supplied via this function's existing data argument (mrgsolve event data, e.g. evid/amt/ cmt/time rows) exactly as for any mrgsolve model; covariates/beta (see "Covariates and the linear predictor" above) compose with these models unchanged – lp is folded into eta the same way the closed-form models do, wherever a given backbone itself multiplies a hazard-scale quantity by eta (verified directly, not assumed, for the models where lp is wired into the hazard link this way). TMDD is the intentionally stiff member of this set (fast binding kinetics next to slow target turnover) and is this library's designated steepness stress case. An outright ODE solver failure (not the reported-grid fallback described above, an mrgsolve/lsoda error that stops the call) is possible for "tmdd_hazard" at a sufficiently extreme parameter/dose combination – far past any shipped default – and is not wrapped with a more informative message: it means the parameters are too extreme for the requested tolerance; try tighter rtol/atol or a smaller dose.

Covariates and the linear predictor

covariates/beta generalize sim_tte()'s single-covariate lp_data mechanism to an arbitrary named set: \(lp(t) = \sum_k \beta_k X_k(t)\), computed in R and supplied to the model as an ordinary time-varying lp covariate (last-observation-carried-forward, the same convention sim_tte() already uses) – no library model file needs to change to support this, since every one of them already recomputes eta = exp(mu + lp) inside $ODE. Coverage follows the same rule as sim_tte()'s Weibull lp_data path: every subject's covariates must include an observation at time = 0; the last known value is carried forward for any remaining follow-up (no M-spline-style "must reach end" requirement, since these are genuine ODE models, not a piecewise-constant-on-a-fixed-grid closed form). Limitation: when covariates has an ID column, it must equal 1:nrow(idata) exactly – subject-specific covariates for a non-default (non-1:n) subject numbering are not yet supported. Combining with data: when a dosing data is also supplied, every dosing record's lp is filled with the covariate value already in force for that subject at that time (the same last-observation-carried-forward rule as above), so a dosing regimen and time-varying covariates compose freely, with no mrgsolve warning. data already carrying its own lp column is an error (which value should apply at a dosing record would otherwise be ambiguous).

Legacy form (formula not supplied): every name in beta must be a raw numeric column of covariates, used as-is – no factor coding, interactions, or transforms.

Formula form: supplying formula builds a design matrix X via model.matrix(formula, covariates), and lp(t) = X(t) %*% beta; beta's names must then match colnames(X) exactly (an error lists the expected names otherwise). covariates may be baseline (no time column – equivalent to a single time = 0 row per subject, carried forward for the whole follow-up) or time-varying (as in the legacy form). A baseline frame with no ID column is either a population-level constant, recycled to every subject, if it has exactly one row, or one row per subject if it has more than one row – in the latter case, n (see above) is inferred from its row count when not supplied explicitly. An implied intercept column is dropped automatically, with a message() naming why (the model's own baseline hazard parameter, e.g. H0/mu, already plays that role, so an intercept in lp would be additively unidentifiable against it) – write formula = ~ 0 + ... to suppress that message and get one design-matrix column per factor level instead of the usual k - 1 treatment-contrast columns for the first factor term in formula (R's own model.matrix convention for keeping a no-intercept design full rank; every other factor term still gets k - 1 columns). A separate message() names which term this happened for, since it changes what beta's expected names are.

Because X only ever needs to be linear in beta, not in the covariates themselves, terms nonlinear in a covariate are in scope: formula = ~ 0 + age + I(age^2) + log(dose) + splines::ns(weight, 3) + arm, or a covariate column already computed as an Emax-shaped transform of a known, fixed EC50 (e.g. a column dose / (EC50 + dose) for a literal numeric EC50), all work directly. Terms nonlinear in a parameter the model itself estimates or a caller varies across scenarios – an Emax link whose EC50 is itself unknown or varied – are out of scope for lp/formula: that belongs in the model's HAZ expression instead (tte_model(hazard = "H0 * (CP / (EC50 + CP))", params = list(EC50 = 5))), where it composes with PK/PD states, BSV, and dosing directly. The two express the same kind of relationship, but only the second lets EC50 itself be estimated or varied; a fixed EC50 can be written either way, and gives the same event-time distribution either way (verified directly).

Between-subject variability

omega adds between-subject variability (BSV) to the structural PK/PD parameters of the six models above (not to H0/lp/beta_*, the hazard-scale parameters this package's own scaffold adds): a log-normal draw, \(\theta_i = \theta_{pop} \cdot \exp(\eta_i)\), computed in R with mvgauss and supplied as ordinary idata columns – exactly the mechanism already used for U (no model file needs a declared $OMEGA block for this to work). The valid targets are every structural parameter of the model's own mrgsolve backbone (see each *_hazard.cpp file's own [PROB] block for the exact list, e.g. pk_hazard: CL, V2, Q, V3, KA, KA2, VMAX, KM).

omega may be named (matching dimnames, any subset of the model's targets, any order – e.g. BSV on CL only) or unnamed (dimension must equal the full target list, applied positionally in the order documented for that model). Population values come from the resolved parameters (param overrides applied first), so param = list(CL = 3) together with omega on "CL" centers the draw on 3. Supplying both an idata column and an omega target with the same name is an error (no silent override in either direction).

Coexistence with a user-supplied model (a compiled mrgmod with its own $OMEGA/ETA() wiring): omega is dispatched on whether the resolved model already declares a matching block. A model that does (any hand-written model using the standard TVCL/ETA() idiom) goes through omat exactly as before – unaffected by this mechanism. Only a model with no declared block falls through to the idata route, and only if it is one of the named models above; omega on any other model (the closed-form-style library models, or a user model with neither) keeps the existing informative error naming the missing $OMEGA block.

sigma is unaffected by any of this and stays exactly what it was: forwarded to smat, usable only for a model (necessarily user-supplied, for now) that already declares a $SIGMA block – no built-in library model's hazard depends on a residual-error-perturbed quantity.

Right censoring

$events always carries sim_reason, distinguishing "event" from administrative censoring at end ("administrative"). Supplying censoring adds a second, independent censoring process on top – a per-subject censoring time drawn from the requested distribution, with the observed outcome becoming min(event time, censoring time, end) and sim_reason = "censored" for a subject pulled earlier by the draw. See add_censoring for the full spec (the same function this argument calls internally); this is applied in R after simulation rather than as a second ODE compartment (out of scope for this release: censoring that depends on a subject's own simulated PK/PD trajectory, e.g. dropout driven by toxicity).

Interval censoring

Supplying visits maps the exact (and, if censoring was also supplied, already right-censored) outcome onto an interval, via add_interval_censoring: an event is only knowable at the first visit at or after it happened, giving (L, R]; a censored subject is only known event-free through their last visit at or before their own censoring time, giving (L, Inf). sim_time/sim_status/sim_reason are unchanged – sim_time_left/sim_time_right are added on top. Always applied after any censoring (see add_interval_censoring "Ordering with right censoring" for why the order matters); a list(every = , jitter = ) value builds the schedule via visit_schedule first, inside this call's own seeded block – a post-simulation R mapping, not an in-solver mechanism.

A realistic (missed-visit, dropout, or outcome-reactive) schedule is not a visits = form this function accepts directly – build it standalone, then pass the result as visits:


sched <- visit_schedule(n = 50, every = 4, end = 24, jitter = 1, seed = 1)
realized <- thin_visits(sched, p_miss = 0.1, seed = 2)
sim <- sim_tte_ode(model = "exponential", param = list(H0 = 0.05),
  n = 50, end = 24, delta = 2, visits = realized, seed = 1)

visit_schedule_informative (which needs $events, so it cannot run before simulation at all) composes the same way, applied to sim$events after the fact and fed back through add_interval_censoring directly rather than through this function's visits argument a second time.

Reproducibility

If idata does not supply U, exactly one stats::runif(1) is drawn per row of idata (one row per subject), in row order, before mrgsolve is called. With a fixed seed (or a set.seed() call by the caller), results are therefore reproducible for a fixed idata row order.

The idata-based omega draw ("Between-subject variability" above) is likewise reproducible for a fixed seed – verified directly (not assumed from mrgsolve's own documentation) that mvgauss's draw, called without its own seed argument, is insensitive to any runif()/rnorm() draws made in between (such as the U draw above), so one seed deterministically reproduces both regardless of draw order.

Parallel simulation

model is a character library name or a simtte_model every time; either way, sim_tte_ode() builds (or reuses an already-built) compiled mrgsolve model and loadsos it before simulating – always, whether or not you prepare anything yourself. On a single process this needs no attention. On a makePSOCKcluster worker – a separate R process, with no memory of what the parent process already built – each worker independently paying its own first-call compile cost is not wrong, just wasteful (harmless for a fast-compiling built-in model; can be a real cost, up to a couple of seconds, for a tte_model-converted one).

simtte_prepare_model builds a model once and returns an object sim_tte_ode() never rebuilds; call it once per worker at cluster initialization, then pass its return value as model in every later sim_tte_ode() call on that worker:


cl <- parallel::makePSOCKcluster(2)
parallel::clusterCall(cl, simtte::simtte_prepare_model,
  model = "irm1_hazard")
results <- parallel::parLapply(cl, seeds, function(s) {
  sim_tte_ode(model = "irm1_hazard", param = list(H0 = 0.01, beta_r = 1),
    n = 50, end = 30, delta = 2, seed = s)
})
parallel::stopCluster(cl)

For a tte_model-converted model, build it once in the parent and broadcast the already-compiled object instead of having every worker convert/compile it independently:


tm <- tte_model(my_model, hazard = "H0 * exp(lp + beta * CP)",
  params = list(H0 = 0.01, beta = 0))
prepared <- simtte_prepare_model(tm)
parallel::clusterCall(cl, simtte::simtte_prepare_model, model = prepared)
results <- parallel::parLapply(cl, seeds, function(s) {
  sim_tte_ode(model = prepared, n = 50, end = 30, delta = 2, seed = s)
})

This is also the only pattern verified race-free under repeated, fresh-cache stress testing: a worker that only ever calls loadso() on an already-compiled object cannot race (a pure read, never a write), unlike a worker independently re-triggering its own build against a directory another process might be writing to at the same time – see the investigation report cited below for the measurements.

For model = "mspline", simtte_prepare_model only takes knots (only its length matters – it selects which shipped variant is compiled); coefs/boundary_knots are supplied to sim_tte_ode() as usual, not to simtte_prepare_model() (see simtte_prepare_model's own documentation for why).

Fork clusters (mclapply, Unix-only): a forked worker inherits the parent process's memory directly, compiled model included, so none of the above is needed – simulate immediately, with no simtte_prepare_model()/clusterCall() step at all.

simtte_model_cache controls where a model is built (default: a directory under tempdir(), i.e. session-scoped and CRAN-safe); see its own documentation for persisting a compiled model across R sessions, and simtte_model_cache_clear to remove what accumulates there (e.g. after an R/simtte/mrgsolve upgrade, for a persistent cache). sim_tte_ode()/simtte_prepare_model() never call options() themselves – mrgsolve.project/mrgsolve.soloc are passed explicitly, never set globally on your behalf.

See also

Choosing a model: sim_tte_ode_models lists the built-in names; tte_model converts your own mrgsolve model into something model accepts. Post-processing the returned $events: add_censoring for independent right censoring (what censoring calls internally; censoring_rate_for helps choose its rate) and add_interval_censoring for assessment-time intervals (what visits calls; build the schedule with visit_schedule). Parallel or multi-process runs: simtte_prepare_model builds a model once per process, simtte_model_cache says where it is stored, and simtte_model_cache_clear removes it (see "Parallel simulation" above). The older grid-based engine: sim_tte and sim_tte_df, which this function does not replace.

Examples

# \donttest{
sim <- sim_tte_ode(model = "exponential", param = list(H0 = 0.1),
  n = 50, end = 30, delta = 5, seed = 1)
#> Loading model from cache.
head(sim$events)
#>   ID   sim_time sim_status sim_reason
#> 1  1 13.2610805          1      event
#> 2  2  9.8852799          1      event
